title: Longitude
say: Tonight is about one number. Not latitude, the easy one. Longitude: how far east or west you are. For most of history, at sea, nobody could find it. Let me show you what that cost.
notes:
Talk: 30 minutes, then 15 minutes of questions.
Keys: → or Space next · ← back · P presenter view (this) · F full screen · B black screen · G overview.
The spine of the talk: longitude is a time problem, and a clock solved it.
cue: Night, a storm at sea. Ships in the rain; distant lightning. Title settles.

title: 22 October 1707
say: October 1707. Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell is bringing the British fleet home from the Mediterranean, after the failed siege of Toulon. Days of storm and cloud. No Sun, no stars: no way to check where they are.
notes:
Toulon, summer 1707: Prince Eugene of Savoy attacked by land, Shovell supported from the sea. The siege failed in August, but the French scuttled much of their own fleet in the harbour to protect it.
Shovell left about 15 ships at Gibraltar and sailed for England in late September with about 21.
Nobody ashore knew where the fleet was day to day: news travelled only by dispatch boats and post riders.
cue: The camera glides in beside the flagship Association.

title: Where they believed they were
say: On the twenty-second, the navigators compare their reckonings. Most agree: they are safely west of Ushant, the island off Brittany, with open water ahead into the Channel.
notes:
Dead reckoning: speed × time × heading, from the last known position. After days of storm, small errors pile up.
The ghost (dashed) fleet is where they believed they were.
cue: Rise out of the storm to a moonlit chart; the ghost fleet (dashed) shows the believed position.

title: Where they really were
say: They were wrong. They were farther north and west, heading straight for the Isles of Scilly, off the tip of Cornwall.
notes: Gold: where they really were. Historians also blame charts that put Scilly in the wrong place, and poor latitude after days without a sight. But the problem no one at sea could solve was longitude.
cue: The real fleet (gold) lies farther north, on the Scilly rocks; the gap between them.

title: As many as 2,000
say: Four ships. Somewhere between fourteen hundred and two thousand men. Shovell himself among them. All because they did not know where they were.
notes: Estimates of the dead range from about 1,400 to 2,000. Shovell’s body washed ashore at Porthellick Cove on St Mary’s.
cue: One by one the lanterns go dark. The toll.

title: Two numbers, one missing
say: A position takes two numbers. In 1707, at sea, one of them was a guess. So let's take them one at a time, starting with the easy one.
cue: Two numbers, and one is a question mark.

title: Latitude Is the Easy One
say: About 325 BC. Pytheas, a Greek from Marseille, measures the noon shadow of a stick at home to work out how far north he is. Then he sails north, past Land's End: the same rocks that will sink Shovell. To say where you are on a ball you need two numbers. Start with the easy one. The Earth spins, so it has two poles and an equator halfway between. Nature drew those. Nobody had to agree on them. Latitude counts from the equator, zero, to the pole, ninety. North or south. One degree of latitude is 60 arcminutes. Each arcminute on the ground is one nautical mile, about 6,076 feet. GIS today: latitude is the Y of every point in your feature layer. Always with N or S, or a minus sign for south.
notes:

title: The Star's Height Is Your Latitude
say: Here is why latitude is easy to measure. Drag the person north. At the equator the Pole Star sits on the horizon. Walk north and it climbs. At the pole it is straight overhead. Predict before I move it: Toronto? About 44 degrees. Washington, about 39. Miami, about 26. Twist: you do not need a map, a clock or a king. One star and one angle, any clear night. That is why latitude was known for two thousand years and longitude was not.

title: About four fists: 39° N
say: From Washington, it's about four fists — call it 39 degrees — and Washington is at 39 degrees north. Rough — but sailors did the same thing with proper instruments, measuring the angle far more precisely.
cue: About four fists ≈ 39°: you are near 39° N.

title: Parallels
say: Two families of lines. Parallels — lines of latitude — run east–west, like rungs on a ladder.
cue: Parallels: lines of latitude.

title: Meridians
say: Meridians — lines of longitude — run from pole to pole.
cue: Meridians: lines of longitude.

title: Unroll the globe
say: Unroll the globe and the lines become a grid.
cue: The globe unrolls into a flat grid.

title: The Bingo card
say: Think of a Bingo card. Latitude calls the row; longitude calls the column. Row 38.9 north, column 77 west: Washington.
cue: Bingo: latitude calls the row, longitude the column.

title: The column was the hard part
say: Calling the row was easy — just look at Polaris. Calling the column was the hard part. That is what killed Shovell's sailors.
cue: The column stays lit: the hard part.

title: Longitude is hidden in time
say: Same latitude, different local noon. Longitude isn't hidden in the stars' height. It is hidden in time.
cue: Same latitude, different local noon: longitude is time.

title: Look down on the North Pole
say: Let's look down on the North Pole.
cue: Globe facing Europe.

title: The conversion
say: So we can convert time straight into longitude. One hour, fifteen degrees. Four minutes, one degree. Four seconds, one minute of arc, which at the equator is about one nautical mile. Remember that one: four seconds, about a mile.
notes:
TIME → LONGITUDE (Earth turns 360° in 24 hours)
1 hour of time = 15° of longitude
4 minutes = 1°
1 minute = 15′ (arcminutes)
4 seconds = 1′
1 second = 15″ (arcseconds)
1′ of longitude ≈ 1 nautical mile at the equator; at Greenwich’s latitude (51.5° N) about 62% of that. So 1 minute of clock error ≈ 15 nautical miles at the equator; 1 second ≈ a quarter mile.
H4: 5 seconds of time = 75″ ≈ 1.25′ of longitude ≈ roughly a nautical mile at the equator (a bit less on the way to Jamaica).
cue: Slide: The conversion

title: Noon in New York
say: Let’s bring it home, to a map we all know. Here is noon arriving at New York, seventy-four degrees west of Greenwich. The Sun is as high as it will get today.
notes: New York City Hall: 40.71° N, 74.01° W. The faint dashed lines are the 75°, 90°, 105° and 120° W meridians: remember them for the railroads.
cue: Fly to North America; the gold noon line arrives at New York. Faint meridians at 75°, 90°, 105°, 120° W.

title: Noon walks west
say: Now watch the Earth keep turning. Noon walks west, steadily. Five minutes after New York, it’s noon in Philadelphia. Twenty-four minutes, Pittsburgh. Fifty-one, Nashville. Just over an hour: Memphis, fifteen degrees. Two hours: Denver, thirty degrees. Three hours: Los Angeles, forty-five. That line is moving at about seven hundred ninety miles an hour.
notes:
SPEED OF NOON: noon (the Sun’s highest point) sweeps west 1° every 4 minutes, 1′ every 4 seconds. At New York’s latitude (40.7° N) that is about 13 miles a minute, roughly 790 mph. At the equator ≈ 1,040 mph; at Greenwich ≈ 650 mph. Every meridian has its own noon: between New York and Memphis there are endless noons.
City noons after New York: Philadelphia +5 min, Pittsburgh +24, Nashville +51, Memphis +64 (≈ 15°), Denver ≈ +2 h (≈ 30°), Los Angeles ≈ +3 h (≈ 45°).

RAILROADS: Until 1883 every town kept its own local noon: hundreds of local times; US railroads ran on dozens of them. On 18 November 1883, the ‘Day of Two Noons’, the railroads switched to four standard zones on the 75°, 90°, 105° and 120° W meridians (William F. Allen’s plan). Towns in the eastern half of each zone set clocks back and heard noon twice. Many towns resisted ‘railroad time’; Congress made it law only in 1918 (Standard Time Act).

JEFF’S TWO TALKING POINTS
1. Denver was ~28° west on many American maps: measured from Washington, D.C. (Naval Observatory, 77°03′ W of Greenwich), not from Greenwich (105° W).
2. The railroads moved first: their 1883 zones were already Greenwich-based, a year before the 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington. That head start helped Greenwich win. France abstained and kept Paris until 1911.
cue: The gold noon line slides west at Earth’s steady rate; each city lights as its noon arrives: Philadelphia +5 min, Pittsburgh +24, Nashville +51, Memphis +64, Denver +2 h, Los Angeles +3 h.

title: The speed of noon
say: Think about that. Noon is racing across the country at about thirteen miles a minute, seven hundred ninety miles an hour at New York. Faster than the plane you flew in on. At the equator it’s over a thousand.
notes:
Equator: 24,901 mi ÷ 24 h ≈ 1,040 mph. × cos(40.7°) ≈ 790 mph at New York (≈ 13 mi/min). × cos(51.5°) ≈ 650 mph at Greenwich. Airliner cruise ≈ 550 mph.
SPEED OF NOON: noon (the Sun’s highest point) sweeps west 1° every 4 minutes, 1′ every 4 seconds. At New York’s latitude (40.7° N) that is about 13 miles a minute, roughly 790 mph. At the equator ≈ 1,040 mph; at Greenwich ≈ 650 mph. Every meridian has its own noon: between New York and Memphis there are endless noons.
City noons after New York: Philadelphia +5 min, Pittsburgh +24, Nashville +51, Memphis +64 (≈ 15°), Denver ≈ +2 h (≈ 30°), Los Angeles ≈ +3 h (≈ 45°).
cue: Slide: 790 mph

title: Every town had its own noon
say: So every town had its own noon, and its own time. When it was noon in New York, Philadelphia’s Sun said five to twelve. Memphis, about four minutes to eleven. Los Angeles, about nine in the morning. Between any two towns there are endless noons. Hold on to that; the railroads will hate it.
notes:
Exact sun-time offsets from New York (74.01° W): PHL 75.17° → −5 min (11:55); PIT 80.0° → −24 (11:36); BNA 86.78° → −51 (11:09); MEM 90.05° → −64 (10:56); DEN 104.99° → −2 h 04 (≈ 9:56); LA 118.24° → −2 h 57 (≈ 9:03).
Every town until 1883 set its clocks by its own noon.
cue: Slide: Every town had its own noon

title: Alone at sea
say: But here is the catch. Take away the cities, the phones, the radio. You are on one small ship in the middle of the Pacific. You can see your own noon: the Sun tells you that. What you cannot see is what time it is back home. And without home’s time, you cannot know how far west you have come.
notes:
This is the eureka: you only know how far you are from home if you know home’s time. On land you could ask; at sea, with no communication, the only way is to carry it.
The ship is at 149° W, 75° west of New York: when its Sun is highest, New York’s clock reads 5 p.m.
cue: Cities and labels fade; the camera drifts out over the empty Pacific to one small ship at its own noon.

title: Compare two clocks
say: So the method is simple. Your noon comes from the Sun. Home’s time comes from a clock you carried with you. If your Sun says noon and the home clock says five, you are five hours, seventy-five degrees, west of home.
notes:
5 h × 15° = 75°. One minute of clock error = 15′ of longitude ≈ 15 nautical miles at the equator.
TIME → LONGITUDE (Earth turns 360° in 24 hours)
1 hour of time = 15° of longitude
4 minutes = 1°
1 minute = 15′ (arcminutes)
4 seconds = 1′
1 second = 15″ (arcseconds)
1′ of longitude ≈ 1 nautical mile at the equator; at Greenwich’s latitude (51.5° N) about 62% of that. So 1 minute of clock error ≈ 15 nautical miles at the equator; 1 second ≈ a quarter mile.
H4: 5 seconds of time = 75″ ≈ 1.25′ of longitude ≈ roughly a nautical mile at the equator (a bit less on the way to Jamaica).
cue: Slide: Compare two clocks

title: Carry home’s time
say: So the answer is simple to say and fiendishly hard to do: carry home’s time with you. A clock set to home, that keeps home’s time all the way across the ocean. Compare it with your own noon, and every hour of difference is fifteen degrees of longitude.
notes: Answer to the twist: a clock that carries home time. The hands show 5:00, New York time, while the ship sees noon: 5 h × 15° = 75° west. (Don’t name the watch or its accuracy here; that comes with H4 and the vote.)
cue: A watch glows in the dark, its hands holding home time (5 o’clock). Bridges to Harrison and H4.

title: Greenwich: zero
say: Here is Greenwich, London's home meridian, at zero. London sees noon first.
cue: Greenwich at zero; noon in London.

title: Two hours later: 30°
say: Two hours later, as Earth turns, the western ship sees noon. Two slices: thirty degrees.
cue: Earth turns two hours: the western ship reaches noon.

title: Local noon vs. London time
say: Stand on that ship when your Sun is highest. Your local time is noon. If a clock from London says two in the afternoon, you are two hours — thirty degrees — west of home.
cue: On the ship: local noon; the London clock reads 14:00, so 30° west.

title: A clock at sea?
say: Simple to say. But a clock at sea? It rolls, it pitches, it gets hot and cold and damp, for months. In 1700 the best clocks were pendulum clocks. Put one on a ship and the pendulum goes crazy.
notes: A pendulum clock good to seconds a day on land could be off by many minutes a day at sea. Newton doubted a sea clock would ever be good enough.
cue: The hard part: keeping home time on a ship at sea.

title: The Longitude Act, 1714
say: Seven years after Scilly, Parliament offered a fortune: up to twenty thousand pounds, millions today, for a practical way to find longitude at sea. The closer you got, the more you won: half a degree, thirty nautical miles, for the top prize.
notes:
Longitude Act 1714: £10,000 within 1° (60 nautical miles), £15,000 within ⅔° (40 nmi), £20,000 within ½° (30 nmi), tested on a voyage to the West Indies. £20,000 in 1714 ≈ £3–4 million today. Administered by the Commissioners (later Board) of Longitude.
Half a degree of longitude = 2 minutes of time.
cue: Slide: The Longitude Act

title: Two ideas
say: There were two ways to get home’s time. Read a clock in the sky, which is what the astronomers wanted. Or carry a clock with you, which is what a Yorkshire carpenter wanted. Let’s start in the sky.
notes: Both methods answer the same question: what time is it at home (Paris, Greenwich) right now?
cue: Slide: Read a clock in the sky, or carry one

title: Galileo’s moons
say: In 1610 Galileo pointed a telescope at Jupiter and found four moons. And he saw something wonderful: they eclipse. Io, the innermost, slips into Jupiter’s shadow every forty-two and a half hours. And everyone who sees it blink out sees it at the same instant. A clock in the sky that the whole Earth can read.
notes: Io’s period: 1.769 days ≈ 42.5 hours. Galileo proposed using the moons for longitude to Spain and later the Dutch, without success at sea.
cue: Slide: Galileo’s moons

title: Io laps every 42½ hours
say: Here’s Jupiter, with its four moons going round like hands on a clock face. Io laps every forty-two and a half hours.
notes: The moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto (the Galilean moons). Jupiter is ~5 times farther from the Sun than Earth.
cue: The moons orbit like clock hands; Io laps every 42.5 hours.

title: Io blinks out
say: Watch Io slide into Jupiter’s shadow. It blinks out. For anyone watching, in Paris, in London, on a mountain in Peru, it happens at the same moment.
notes: The eclipse is a universal signal, like a time pip on the radio, centuries early. Note: strictly it is seen at the same instant everywhere on Earth, give or take light travel across Earth (0.04 s).
cue: Io slips into Jupiter’s shadow: the same instant for every observer.

title: France got smaller
say: On land it worked beautifully. Jean Picard and the Cassini team timed Io from points all around France. Their new map moved the whole west coast east, by a degree and a half in places. France got smaller.
notes: Picard and La Hire’s survey from 1679, under the Paris Observatory of Giovanni Domenico Cassini. The corrected map was presented in 1693.
cue: Slide: France got smaller

title: Aside: Rømer, Light Needs Time
say: An aside on Jupiter's clock. Paris, 1676. Ole Rømer is timing the eclipses of Io against the printed table. When the Earth is moving away from Jupiter, the eclipses come late. When it is coming back, they come early. Move the Earth round. On the far side the news is more than sixteen minutes behind. Twist: Io is on time. The light is late. Rømer had found that light takes time to travel.
notes:
Source speaker notes (Claude v3):

When the Earth is moving away from Jupiter, the eclipses come late. When it is coming back, they come early.

title: Not on a rolling ship
say: But here’s the problem. You need a long telescope, held steady on a tiny moon, on a deck that never stops moving. At sea, it was nearly impossible. Jupiter remapped the land. It couldn’t save a ship.
notes: Galileo even designed a helmet telescope (the celatone) for use at sea. It did not work.
cue: Great on land; nearly impossible from a rolling deck.

title: The Moon drifts across the stars
say: At sea, astronomers tried using our own Moon as the clock hand. The Moon drifts across the stars by about its own width every hour.
cue: The Moon drifts against the stars.

title: Lunar distances
say: Measure the angle between the Moon and a bright star, look it up in tables, and you can work out London time. In principle. In practice it meant hours of arithmetic, from a deck that will not hold still.
cue: Lunar distance: an angle, then hours of arithmetic.

title: Way 2: The Moon
say: Way two: read home time off the Moon. Its champion: Nevil Maskelyne. On a 1761 voyage to St Helena he tests the method. In 1765 he becomes Astronomer Royal. The Moon slides past the stars about half a degree every hour. Measure the angle from the Moon to a star, look it up in a table, and you have Greenwich time. Now roll the deck. You are holding a sextant on a moving ship, trying to touch the Moon to a star. Then the arithmetic: refraction, parallax, the almanac every three hours. An hour or more by candlelight. One arcminute wrong in the sighting is about thirty miles. Twist: the man who backed the Moon becomes a judge of the prize, and so a judge of Harrison's clock.

title: John Harrison
say: And a self-taught carpenter from Yorkshire, John Harrison, decided the answer wasn't in the sky at all. It was a clock.
cue: John Harrison, carpenter and clockmaker.

title: H1, H2, H3
say: He spent thirty years on it. H1, H2, H3: big, beautiful sea clocks, each better than the last. H3 alone took him about nineteen years.
notes: H1 (1730–35) was tested on a voyage to Lisbon in 1736 and did well. H2 (1737–39) was never sent to sea. H3 (1740–59) introduced the bimetallic strip and the caged roller bearing, still used today.
cue: Slide: H1, H2, H3

title: H4
say: This is H4, finished in 1759. About five inches across. It looks like a big pocket watch, and it ticks five times a second. In 1761 it sailed from Portsmouth for Jamaica: eighty-one days at sea.
notes: H4: about 13 cm (5.2 in) across, 1.45 kg. Balance beats 5 times a second (18,000 beats an hour). Voyage on HMS Deptford, November 1761 to January 1762, with Harrison’s son William.
cue: H4 in 3D, turning slowly: the dial, the blued hands. 81 days to Jamaica.

title: Vote: how much did it lose?
say: So here’s my question for you. After eighty-one days at sea, rolling and pitching, how much time do you think H4 had lost? An hour? Ten minutes? A minute? Hands up.
notes:
THE VOTE. Take a few guesses from the room. Do not give the answer on this beat.
Prompts: an hour? ten minutes? a minute? less?
cue: THE VOTE. Camera turns to the movement: gears turning, the balance beating. No answer shown.

title: About five seconds
say: About five seconds. Five seconds in eighty-one days at sea.
notes:
About 5.1 seconds lost in 81 days (after allowing for its known rate).
H4's 5-second error on the Jamaica voyage was 75″, about 1.25′ of longitude. That's roughly a nautical mile at the equator and a bit less on the way to Jamaica.
cue: Reveal: about five seconds in 81 days. Photo of the real H4.

title: No natural zero
say: Now a strange thing. Latitude has a natural zero — the equator. Longitude doesn't. Every meridian runs pole to pole; not one is special.
cue: The equator is natural; the meridians are all equal.

title: Where would you put zero?
say: So, a question for the room: if you were in charge, where would you put zero? Your hometown? Your chapter headquarters? Shout it out, or drop it in the chat.
cue: Ask the room: where would you put zero?

title: Every country had its own zero
say: There was one more problem. Latitude has a natural zero, the equator. Longitude doesn’t. So every country picked its own: Paris for the French, Greenwich for the British, Washington on many American maps, and older European maps used Ferro in the Canary Islands. The same city had a different longitude on every map.
notes:
Paris Observatory 2°20′14″ E of Greenwich. US Naval Observatory (old) 77°03′ W. Ferro (El Hierro), conventionally exactly 20° W of Paris = 17°40′ W of Greenwich. Spain: Cádiz / San Fernando (≈ 6°12′ W). Russia: Pulkovo (30°19′ E). About 72% of the world’s shipping already used Greenwich-based charts.
JEFF’S TWO TALKING POINTS
1. Denver was ~28° west on many American maps: measured from Washington, D.C. (Naval Observatory, 77°03′ W of Greenwich), not from Greenwich (105° W).
2. The railroads moved first: their 1883 zones were already Greenwich-based, a year before the 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington. That head start helped Greenwich win. France abstained and kept Paris until 1911.
cue: Slide: Every country had its own zero

title: Denver: 105° or 28°?
say: Here’s my favourite example. From Greenwich, Denver is a hundred and five degrees west. But on many American maps of the 1800s, Denver was about twenty-eight degrees west: west of Washington. Same city, two numbers. You had to know whose zero you were using.
notes:
JEFF’S TWO TALKING POINTS
1. Denver was ~28° west on many American maps: measured from Washington, D.C. (Naval Observatory, 77°03′ W of Greenwich), not from Greenwich (105° W).
2. The railroads moved first: their 1883 zones were already Greenwich-based, a year before the 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington. That head start helped Greenwich win. France abstained and kept Paris until 1911.
Denver 104.99° W − Washington 77.05° W ≈ 27.9° W of Washington.
cue: Slide: Denver: 105°, or 28°?

title: Washington, October 1884
say: So in October 1884, twenty-five nations sent delegates to Washington to pick one zero for the whole world.
notes:
International Meridian Conference, Washington, D.C., 1–22 October 1884, called by President Chester Arthur. 41 delegates from 25 nations.
AFTER 1884: the conference adopted Greenwich and a universal day, but NOT Fleming’s zones. Countries joined one by one: Japan 1888, much of Europe in the 1890s, France 1911, the Netherlands 1940. Oddities today: India +5½, Nepal +5¾, and all of China on one zone though it spans about five.
cue: Slide: One zero for the world

title: Washington, 1884: Where Is Zero?
say: Here is the globe version of that choice. Greenwich was already used on most shipping charts. The conference formalized a convention, not a law of nature.
notes:
Source speaker notes (Claude v3):
1876, Ireland. The engineer Sandford Fleming misses a train because the printed timetable said p.m. instead of a.m. He spends eight years campaigning for standard time.
October 1884, Washington. Twenty-five nations meet at the International Meridian Conference, Fleming among the delegates. Vote: Greenwich, Paris, Washington, or Ferro in the Canaries, the old zero of many maps.
Press 1, Greenwich: 22 to 1. San Domingo votes against. France and Brazil abstain.
Why Greenwich? About seven in ten of the world's ships already used Greenwich charts. The vote was won before the meeting began.
Press And France? France keeps Paris time until 1911, and even then calls it Paris time, retarded by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds.
Twist: power decides zero. GIS today: the zero in your GPS and in WGS 84 runs about 102 meters, 335 feet, east of the old line at Greenwich.
Keep this recap brief; the preceding slide establishes the meeting, and the next gives the vote.
cue: Interactive slide: Washington, 1884: Where Is Zero?

title: Greenwich wins: 22 votes
say: Greenwich won, twenty-two votes to one, with two abstentions. Most of the world’s ships already used Greenwich charts. And the American railroads had set their time zones on Greenwich a year earlier. That head start helped Greenwich win.
notes:
Vote on Greenwich as prime meridian: 22 for, 1 against (San Domingo, today’s Dominican Republic), 2 abstentions (France, Brazil).
AFTER 1884: the conference adopted Greenwich and a universal day, but NOT Fleming’s zones. Countries joined one by one: Japan 1888, much of Europe in the 1890s, France 1911, the Netherlands 1940. Oddities today: India +5½, Nepal +5¾, and all of China on one zone though it spans about five.

JEFF’S TWO TALKING POINTS
1. Denver was ~28° west on many American maps: measured from Washington, D.C. (Naval Observatory, 77°03′ W of Greenwich), not from Greenwich (105° W).
2. The railroads moved first: their 1883 zones were already Greenwich-based, a year before the 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington. That head start helped Greenwich win. France abstained and kept Paris until 1911.
cue: Gold arcs fly to Greenwich: 22 votes for.

title: Paris held out
say: France abstained, and kept Paris time until 1911. And even then, the French law didn’t say Greenwich. It said Paris mean time, slowed down by nine minutes twenty-one seconds. Which is Greenwich.
notes:
French law of 9 March 1911: legal time = “temps moyen de Paris, retardé de neuf minutes vingt et une secondes”. France’s own survey maps kept a Paris meridian (in grads) much longer.
AFTER 1884: the conference adopted Greenwich and a universal day, but NOT Fleming’s zones. Countries joined one by one: Japan 1888, much of Europe in the 1890s, France 1911, the Netherlands 1940. Oddities today: India +5½, Nepal +5¾, and all of China on one zone though it spans about five.
cue: Slide: Paris held out

title: The zones today
say: Here’s the map today. Four zones, still one hour apart. Each little clock sits right on its zone’s meridian: seventy-five west near Philadelphia, ninety near Memphis, one-oh-five at Denver, one-twenty near Fresno. On that line, clock noon is Sun noon. Everywhere else, your clock is off the Sun, by up to half an hour or more. And look how the edges bend: they follow state and county lines, not meridians.
notes:
WHY THE CLOCKS SIT ON THE MERIDIANS: only along each zone’s central meridian (75°, 90°, 105°, 120° W) does clock noon equal Sun noon. Away from it, the Sun is early (east) or late (west) by 4 minutes per degree: up to ~30 minutes at the ideal ±7.5° edges, more where zones bend.
In theory each zone is ±7.5° wide; in practice the boundaries bend to state and county lines (Detroit on Eastern, El Paso on Mountain; most of Arizona skips daylight saving).
On the USGS National Atlas map the clocks are simply placed mid-zone for display; here they sit exactly on the meridians.
ZONES TODAY: centred on multiples of 15° from Greenwich: Eastern 75° W (UTC−5), Central 90° W (−6), Mountain 105° W (−7), Pacific 120° W (−8). In theory ±7.5° wide; in practice bent to state and county lines (Detroit on Eastern, El Paso on Mountain; Arizona skips DST).
DOWD & FLEMING: Dowd argued for the US only, and his first plan (~1870) used the Washington meridian, not Greenwich. Sandford Fleming, a Canadian railway engineer, pushed 24 world zones from 1879.
cue: A plain US map: four muted zone bands following the real (bent) borders, gold meridians at 75°, 90°, 105° and 120° W, a clock on each meridian near Philadelphia, Memphis, Denver and Fresno.

title: 32 satellites, six planes
say: By 1995 GPS was declared fully operational. Today there are 32 active satellites in six orbital planes, each one circling the Earth twice a day.
cue: 1995 → today: 32 satellites, six planes, twice a day around Earth.

title: A sky full of clocks
say: And today? Look up. Thirty-one or so GPS satellites, and every one carries atomic clocks and broadcasts, nonstop: who it is, where it is, and exactly what time it is. A sky full of Harrison’s clocks.
notes: GPS: about 31 operational satellites (the constellation design is 24+), six orbital planes, ~20,200 km up, each orbiting twice a day. Each carries rubidium and/or caesium atomic clocks.
cue: Every satellite broadcasts its time: pulses ripple out.

title: The fourth satellite
say: Your phone hears four of them. Each signal says when it left; the delay tells you how far away that satellite is. Three distances give your place. The fourth fixes your phone’s own cheap clock. Still the same trick: position from time.
notes: Four unknowns: x, y, z and the receiver’s clock error. Four satellites → four equations. That is why GPS needs at least four.
cue: The fourth satellite solves the clock: the rings snap to one spot.

title: The Date Line
say: July 1522, the Cape Verde islands. Magellan's last surviving ship comes home round the world. The log says Wednesday. The people on shore say Thursday. They lost a day going west. If zero is at Greenwich, the other side of the world is 180 degrees. Someone has to start the new day. Press 2, Alaska. Russia sells Alaska to the United States in 1867, and Alaska switches from Russia's side of the line to America's. In Sitka, Friday happens twice. Press 3, Kiribati. It straddled the line, so half the country was a day apart from the other half. In 1995 the line moved east around it; the eastern islands skipped December 31, 1994. Press 4, Samoa. Samoa trades mostly with Australia and New Zealand, so in 2011 it jumps the line. Thursday the 29th is followed by Saturday the 31st. American Samoa, about 80 miles away, stays a day behind. Twist: the date line is a political line, not a meridian. GIS today: data that crosses 180 degrees, like the Aleutians or Fiji, breaks maps unless you handle the antimeridian.

title: Appendix: What Each Decimal Place Buys
say: If someone asks why GPS shows so many decimals: each decimal place makes the circle ten times smaller. Press up to add a place, down to take one away. No decimals: you are somewhere in a circle about 69 miles across New York. Two: about 0.7 mile. Four: about 36 feet, the plaza. Six: about 4 inches. For a Red Cross address, four decimals is the building; five is the door. More than six is noise from the receiver, not real precision.

title: Appendix: Null Island
say: If someone asks why points show up off Africa: 0 degrees latitude, 0 degrees longitude. Open ocean in the Gulf of Guinea, and one weather buoy. A failed geocode, a blank cell in a spreadsheet, a GPS left off. Every one of them is read as 0, 0, and lands right here. So a point at Null Island is not a place. It is a failure that looks like a place. Filter for 0, 0 before you map anything.

title: Appendix: Rømer, Light Needs Time
say: Same scene as in the talk, for questions. Earth near Jupiter: the eclipse is on time. Months later the Earth is on the far side of the Sun. The eclipse is about 16 and a half minutes late: the light crosses the whole orbit. Io is on time. The light is late.

title: Galileo's Moons
say: Day two: measuring the heavens. We start in January 1610. Galileo turns a telescope on Jupiter and sees three small stars in a line. The next night they have moved. Soon there are four. Step through the nights and keep his notebook. They are not stars. They are moons, going round Jupiter. Before you see the answer, make a guess: which moon goes round fastest? Each moon keeps strict time. That makes Jupiter a clock that anyone on Earth can read. Yesterday we saw why that matters.

title: Appendix: One Degree More
say: Only if the room asks. One turn of the Earth against the stars takes 23 hours 56 minutes. Press One Turn. The far star is back overhead. But the Earth has moved along its orbit, so the Sun is not. Press One More Degree. The Earth turns about one more degree to face the Sun again. One degree is four minutes. That is the 24-hour day.
